questions.question_text: Which of these is **not** modelled as a projectile?

options.text: A jet aircraft cruising with its engines running
A cricket ball after being hit by the bat
options.why: Once the ball leaves the bat the only force acting on it is gravity, so it is a projectile.

options.text: An arrow after it leaves the bow
options.why: The bow no longer acts on the arrow, so gravity alone acts and the arrow is a projectile.

options.text: A stone dropped from a bridge
options.why: A dropped stone falls under gravity alone; a projectile need not be launched at an angle.

questions.solution_text:
A cruising jet has thrust from its engines as well as gravity acting on it.
The jet aircraft is not a projectile.

questions.question_text: The simple projectile model assumes that air resistance is negligible. Which statement is a consequence of that assumption?

options.text: The only force acting during the flight is gravity.
The projectile travels in a straight line.
options.why: Confuses no resistance with no force at all; gravity still curves the path into a parabola.
Applies the constant-horizontal-velocity result to the vertical component, which gravity changes.
Assumes a drag force still slows the horizontal motion, but the model has removed that force.

questions.solution_text: Removing air resistance leaves gravity as the only force acting on the projectile.

questions.question_text: A ball is projected at $35^{\circ}$ above the horizontal with speed $22\text{ m/s}$. Take $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$, with up as positive. What are $\ddot{x}$ and $\ddot{y}$?

options.why: Resolved gravity along the launch direction instead of using the whole downward value.
Resolved gravity into both components, but gravity acts vertically only.
Applied gravity to the horizontal component as well, but there is no horizontal force.

questions.question_text: A ball is thrown into the air and reaches the highest point of its flight. Take $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$, with $\underset{\sim}{j}$ pointing **downwards** as the positive vertical direction. Which vector is the acceleration of the ball at that instant?

options.why: Wrote the usual $-g\underset{\sim}{j}$ from memory without noticing that this stem takes downwards as positive.
Put the gravity term in the horizontal component instead of the vertical one.
Both slips at once: gravity placed horizontally and copied with the sign of the up-positive convention.

questions.solution_text:
The acceleration of a projectile is constant, and gravity acts downwards at every instant, including the highest point.
Downwards is positive here, so the vertical component is $+10$.
$\underset{\sim}{\ddot{r}}=0\underset{\sim}{i}+10\underset{\sim}{j}$
$=10\underset{\sim}{j}$

questions.question_text: A ball is thrown with speed $40\text{ m/s}$ at $30^{\circ}$ above the horizontal. Which is $\underset{\sim}{v}(0)$ in exact form?

options.why: Swapped sine and cosine when resolving the initial speed.
Made the vertical component negative, although the ball is thrown upwards.
Both slips: the ratios swapped and the upward component taken as negative.

questions.question_text: A ball is thrown from the top of a wall $5\text{ m}$ above the ground with speed $14\text{ m/s}$ at $20^{\circ}$ above the horizontal. Taking the origin at the foot of the wall, which pair is correct?

options.why: Assumed launch from ground level, losing the $5\text{ m}$ height of the wall.
Swapped sine and cosine when resolving the initial speed.
Both slips: the launch height ignored and the two components swapped.

questions.question_text: A stone is thrown from a cliff at $28^{\circ}$ **below** the horizontal with speed $15\text{ m/s}$. Take $g=10\text{ m/s}^{2}$. Which statement about the horizontal motion holds throughout the flight?

options.text: $\dot{x}=15\cos 28^{\circ}-10t$, because gravity acts on both components.
options.why: Applied the vertical acceleration to the horizontal component, but $\ddot{x}=0$.
Resolved the horizontal component with sine instead of cosine.

options.text: $\dot{x}=15\sin 28^{\circ}-10t$, because gravity acts on both components.
options.why: Both slips: sine used for cosine and gravity applied horizontally.

questions.solution_text:
$\ddot{x}=0$
$\dot{x}=15\cos 28^{\circ}$
The horizontal velocity is unchanged for the whole flight.

questions.question_text: A projectile is launched from the origin with initial velocity $\underset{\sim}{v}(0)=-9\underset{\sim}{i}+12\underset{\sim}{j}$ metres per second. What is its launch speed and direction, with the angle to 1 d.p.?

options.text: $15\text{ m/s}$, at $53.1^{\circ}$ above the horizontal, moving to the left
$15\text{ m/s}$, at $36.9^{\circ}$ above the horizontal, moving to the left
options.why: Used $\tan\alpha=\frac{9}{12}$, inverting the ratio of vertical to horizontal component.

options.text: $21\text{ m/s}$, at $53.1^{\circ}$ above the horizontal, moving to the left
options.why: Added the two component sizes instead of using Pythagoras to find the speed.

options.text: $21\text{ m/s}$, at $36.9^{\circ}$ above the horizontal, moving to the left
options.why: Both slips: components added for the speed and the tangent ratio inverted.

questions.solution_text:
$V=\sqrt{(-9)^{2}+12^{2}}$
$=\sqrt{225}$
$=15$
$\tan\alpha=\dfrac{12}{9}$
$\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)$
$\approx 53.1^{\circ}$
The launch speed is $15\text{ m/s}$ at $53.1^{\circ}$ above the horizontal, directed to the left.
